title: Google's TPU in Orbit Answers Its First Prompt With a Haiku
excerpt: Google says the Project Suncatcher prototype, launched October 1 with four TPUs aboard, generated a Gemma 4 haiku in orbit — a first test, not a working space data center.
body:
• According to Google, its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has produced the first-ever AI response from a data center class TPU in orbit.
  • Engineers uplinked a prompt during a ground-station pass; the onboard Gemma 4 open model generated a haiku about being in space, downlinked as the satellite passed Svalbard, Norway.
  • The prototype launched on October 1, built with Planet and carrying four TPUs, according to GCN's reporting on the mission.
  • Google's next tests examine how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation in orbit, ahead of a planned twin interconnected satellites milestone in 2027.

Google's experiment in running AI compute in space has answered its first prompt. According to a post on its official blog, Google reached what it calls its "Hello World" milestone for Project Suncatcher: the first-ever AI response from a data center class TPU in orbit.

During a ground-station pass, Google uplinked its first prompt to the onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space. As the satellite passed by Svalbard, Norway, the downlinked poem read: "Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core." Google said it then tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems.

What is flying

The prototype satellite launched on October 1 for Project Suncatcher, which Google describes as a long-term research moonshot to explore powering AI compute in space. In the weeks after launch, Google said it completed a commissioning checklist that included powering up the host and TPU trays and running early machine learning tests.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DeSuiavml1p/

According to GCN, the satellite was built with Earth-imaging company Planet and lifted off aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. It carries four Tensor Processing Units, the custom chips Google designed for machine learning and already deploys in data centers on Earth. GCN reported the satellite is in a sun-synchronous orbit, where its solar panels will almost never be in shade, and that the chips will run a version of the Gemma model for 15 minutes at a time because of heat management constraints.

"The sun puts out almost all of the power in our solar system. All of the other power sources that humanity has tapped into are just a tiny fraction of a percent."

— Travis Beals, senior director and lead of Project Suncatcher, quoted by GCN

A test flight, not a working data center

Google has been explicit that this is an early feasibility check rather than a functioning compute cluster. GCN reported that Beals called the satellite "a very minimal test" to make sure the chips can run in space, and that the goal is for the mission to be operational for a year. Because space lacks airflow for cooling, GCN reported Google called cooling the chips "a crucial research challenge" and is working on approaches including pipes and radiators to move heat away from the chips.

Google first described the Project Suncatcher concept in a research blog post in November 2025, outlining a vision for compact satellite constellations linked by laser-based optical communication that could one day scale machine learning compute in orbit, according to GCN.

What happens next

Google said it will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. Verifying that TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space, the company said, paves the way for its next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027. GCN reported Google has not said when, or whether, the concept could move beyond prototype testing toward an operational orbital compute system.
